title: MB2-03193
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, XXXX XXXX, is a citizen of India. He is basing his claim on section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

A friend of the claimant's brother named XXXX had problems with the police in 2011. They suspected him of having ties to terrorists, and they turned to the claimant's brother when XXXX left the country.
The claimant's brother left India for the United States in XXXX 2011 because he could no longer bear the pressure from police, who then turned against the other members of the claimant's family.
The claimant came to Canada in XXXX 2011 to take part in XXXX XXXX XXXX. Afterwards, he returned to India.
In XXXX 2011, the claimant was arrested and detained for XXXX days by police officers who accused him having ties with militants abroad.
The claimant went to Delhi to wait to be able to leave India. He arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2012, and claimed refugee protection around two weeks later.
He fears returning to India, over three years after he left, because he believes the police still want to go after him.

Having analyzed all the evidence, including the claimant's testimony, the panel determines that he is not a "Convention refugee" under section 96 of the IRPA or a "person in need of protection" within the meaning of subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.
The panel is satisfied as to the claimant's identity based on the documents filed on the record, including a copy of his passport.
The claimant testified at the hearing. The panel noted a number of points that undermine his credibility.

The claimant stated that XXXX, a Muslim friend of his older brother XXXX, had problems with the police starting in 2011. They all lived in the same village, which, according to the claimant, has around XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX residents.

The claimant submitted that the police accused XXXX of having ties to terrorists and that after he left the village, the police turned to XXXX, whom they harassed and arrested a number of times so that he would provide information on XXXX and the supposed plans of the militants. On at least three occasions, the claimant's father allegedly had to pay bribes for his son XXXX to be released. Apparently, the pressure was such that XXXX left India for the United States in XXXX 2010.

After XXXX left the village, the police allegedly came after the claimant's family. The claimant described operations that took place at his house during which the police arrived in three or four vehicles, surrounded the house, asked questions, searched, and mistreated his family. They were always trying to find out more about the terrorists' plans. Each time, his father had to pay bribes for them to leave. The claimant stated that he was present for at least two of these operations. He was asked questions about XXXX, XXXX and the terrorists' plans.

However, the claimant came to Canada in XXXX 2011 to participate in XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX He stayed in the country for about three days without claiming refugee protection. He claimed that he then returned to India because he had no intention of staying in Canada. He acknowledged that his brother had sought refuge in the United States then but submitted that he had no direct problems.

The claimant stated that he was arrested and detained by police for XXXX days in XXXX 2011. When the panel asked him whether he was arrested on other occasions, the claimant avoided the question, hesitated, and delayed. He finally answered that he had been arrested and taken to the station on other occasions. He explained that these two arrests are not in his narrative attached to his Personal Information Form (PIF) because of an oversight. He supposedly [translation] "forgot" to write them down because he had been focusing on his arrest.

The claimant stated that he stayed in Delhi for six (6) months waiting to obtain the documents that would allow him to return to Canada. He supposedly did not have any problems during his stay. He stated that this is because he was in hiding.

The panel considers the fact that the claimant did not claim refugee protection when he travelled to Canada in XXXX 2011 to be behaviour that is inconsistent with that of someone who fears for his life. It finds it implausible, in the particular circumstances of this case, that the claimant made the decision to return home because he did not feel targeted, even though, according to his statements, the police had harassed his brother to the point that he left India for the United States and had carried out several large-scale operations at his home.

The panel also does not believe that the failure to indicate in his PIF that he was arrested on two other occasions can be attributed to an [translation] "oversight." Instead, it considers this an attempt to embellish his story during the hearing.

In addition, the panel considers the fact that the claimant stayed in Delhi for six months without experiencing any problems to be an indication that the police are not interested in him outside his village.
The panel draws a negative inference from these points. This inference affects its analysis of whether there is an internal flight alternative in Delhi.

The test for a flight alternative is two-pronged. First, the panel must examine whether there is a location where the claimant could safely relocate. Second, it must determine whether it is unreasonable to expect the claimant to relocate to that safe location.

When asked what would happen to him if he returned to live in Delhi or Mumbai, three years after having left, the claimant responded that he would have to register to work and live in those locations, which would mean that his personal information could be communicated to the police and he could be put in danger again.
The panel does not agree.

The claimant's story indicates that it was the local police who were interested in his brother, and then in his family and in him, and that bribes were paid to them on multiple occasions. When the panel wanted him to explain how the police had paid visits to his family on multiple occasions and then left them alone after a bribe was paid, the claimant answered that [translation] "that is how things work in India, they harass people to get money, it is a business."

From this perspective, the panel finds that the claimant has failed to discharge his burden of demonstrating that Delhi is not a safe location where he could relocate. It does not see how, three years after leaving, the claimant could be of sufficient interest to the local authorities in his village-which is in a different state-for them to deploy the necessary resources to search for him, whereas they had actually profited from the situation to squeeze bribes from the family. Furthermore, it considers the claimant's allegations that his registering in Delhi would result in the corrupt authorities of his village being able to locate him to be speculation, since nothing indicates that his personal information is flagged and would necessarily come to their attention.

Moreover, the panel notes that the claimant stated that his family still lives in the state of Haryana, three years later. The claimant submits that they had to move to a different community because they were still being harassed by the local authorities. However, when the panel asked him to explain how they were still living in the same state without experiencing any problems, the claimant responded that his father has XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX to pay for expenses and that Haryana is a large state. The panel sees this simply as an indication that the claimant would be able to relocate elsewhere.

For all these reasons, the panel rejects the claimant's refugee protection claim.
